food.text: Dʿmt was a kingdom in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia that existed during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. Its people developed irrigation schemes and used plows, which are early signs of organized farming.
The Land of Punt was an ancient kingdom known from Ancient Egyptian trade records. It produced and exported gold, aromatic resins, blackwood, ebony, ivory and wild animals.

Richard Pankhurst observed that early references to Axumite wine can be found in one of the stele erected by the 4th century ruler Ezana. This links the ruler of Aksum to a wine tradition in the kingdom.
With its capital probably at Yeha, the kingdom of Dʿmt grew millet. It also made iron tools and weapons, so its farming and metalworking developed together.

The Aksumites built trade connections between the Indian subcontinent and the Roman Empire via the Silk Road. They primarily exported ivory, tortoise shell, gold and emeralds, and imported silk and spices.

Dʿmt, a kingdom in Eritrea and northern Ethiopia in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, was probably ruled from Yeha. Its people developed irrigation schemes, used plows, grew millet, and made iron tools and weapons.
Aksumite viticulture is also attested by carvings on the base of the great 3rd century obelisk at Axum. The monument therefore preserves evidence of wine-growing in stone.

In December 2020, primatologists from Dartmouth College examined mummified baboons from New Kingdom and Ptolemaic sites in Egypt that were believed to have come from Punt. They were all hamadryas baboons, and the strontium ratio in their tooth enamel showed they were born in an area stretching across present day Eritrea, Ethiopia and north western Somalia.

art.text: The Great Temple of Yeha is a Sabaean-style temple dated to the 7th or 8th century BCE. At 14 metres (46 ft), it is the tallest of any preserved temple of its kind. Its limestone ashlars show typical Sabaean stonemasonry.
art.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

art.text: Among the most spectacular Aksumite survivals are the giant stelae, called hawilts. One of them, now fallen, is the single largest monolithic structure ever erected, or attempted to be erected. Scholars think it may have fallen during or immediately after its erection.

Aksumite architecture flourished from the 4th century BC onward. Most palaces, villas and houses were built of alternating layers of stone and wood. The protruding wooden support beams became known as "monkey heads" and are a staple of Aksumite architecture.

The ruined multi-story tower at Yeha, dated to the 8th century BC, is the best known building of its period in the region. It is believed to have been the capital of Dʿmt. Sabaeans from modern-day Yemen built it and dedicated it to the lunar deity Almaqah.

Coins showing the royal portrait began to be minted in Aksum under King Endybis toward the end of the 3rd century CE. These coins put the ruler's image into circulation alongside the kingdom's growing trade.

The exterior wall of the Great Temple of Yeha resembles the Almaqah temple in Sirwah and the Temple of Awwam in Yemen's Marib Governorate. Its interior layout is similar to the Bar'an Temple in Marib. A building likely stood there before, and some have questioned whether the temple was ever completed.
art.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

art.text: Aksumite monumental building included massive underground tombs, often located beneath stelae. One well-known monolithic example is the "Tomb of the False Door" in Axum.

Aksumite houses were one-room stone structures, two-storey square houses, or roundhouses of sandstone with basalt foundations. Villas were generally two to four storeys tall and built on sprawling rectangular plans, as at the Dungur ruins.

A bronze sceptre or wand discovered at Atsbi Dera carries an inscription mentioning "GDR of Axum". GDR is a ruler also named in southern Arabian inscriptions celebrating victories over him, dated to around the beginning of the 3rd century CE.

At Mezber in eastern Tigray, a large building possibly used as an elite residence dates to between 800 and 750 BCE. It lacks Sabaean influence, suggesting that not every grand structure of the period followed South Arabian models.
art.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

war.text: Around 200 AD, the Kingdom of Aksum reached across the Red Sea into Southern Arabia. There it engaged in conflicts with Saba and Himyar, forming different alliances with chief kingdoms and tribes. Aksum-Himyar conflicts persisted throughout the 3rd century.

The Aksumite Kingdom rose to power in the first century AD in what is now the Tigray Region, with its capital at Aksum. It grew into a major power on the Red Sea, subjugating South Arabia and Meroe and the areas around it.
After Negus Ezana conquered Meroë in 330 AD, he took the title "king of Ethiopia" from the Nubians. The Byzantine Greeks then also began calling the Aksumites Ethiopians.

During the early third century, the Aksumite kings GDRT and ʽDBH sent military expeditions to Arabia. Local Arabian inscriptions call them "nagasi of Aksum and Habashat," and Aksum appears to have established itself in al-Maafer.

Under King Gedara (c. 200–230), the first Aksumite king involved in South Arabian affairs, Aksum controlled much of western Yemen, including the Tihama, Najran and Zafar. A joint Himyarite-Sabean alliance eventually pushed the Aksumites out.

A Greek inscription in Eritrea, the Monumentum Adulitanum, was recorded by Cosmas Indicopleustes. It says that in the mid to late third century an anonymous Aksumite king achieved significant expansion in the Ethiopian Highlands and Arabia, reaching as far as Lake Tana and the borders of Egypt.

Later in the third century, inscriptions mention the kings of Habashat DTWNS and ZQRNS fighting in Arabia. They appear in the record as the mlky hhst dtwns wzqrns, a further sign of Aksum's long involvement in Arabian wars.

literature.text: Ethiopian literature begins with Axumite texts written in the Geʽez language using the Geʽez script, which is indigenous to both Ethiopia and Eritrea. Almost all texts from this early Aksumite period are Christian in nature and were translated from Greek.

Ethiopian historical writing began with inscriptions commissioned by Aksumite monarchs to recount the deeds of their reign. Written in Ge'ez, Greek, or both, they survive on stelae, thrones, and obelisks across Sudan, Eritrea, and Ethiopia.
The Kingdom of Aksum had its own alphabet, the Geʽez script. Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, considered Aksum one of the four great powers of the 3rd century, alongside Persia, Rome, and China.
Ge'ez literature began with Christianity being declared the state religion around 340 AD by King Ezana. Up till the 4th century, Aksumite royal inscriptions are commonly in both Greek and Ge'ez.
The Ethiopic Bible contains 81 books, 46 of the Old Testament and 35 of the New. Its translation was likely begun soon after 350 and was complete by the end of the 5th century.

The Book of Enoch is notable because its complete text has survived in no other language than Geʽez. For other works such as Jubilees and the Ascension of Isaiah, the Ethiopic version is highly regarded as a witness to the original text.

Writing was introduced to Ethiopia as far back as the 5th century BC with the ancient South Arabian script. This script served as the basis for the Geʽez script, whose oldest evidence was found in Matara, Eritrea, and dated to the 2nd century AD.

The 4th-century stelae erected by Ezana of Axum memorialize his battles and his expansion in the Horn of Africa. The Monumentum Adulitanum, inscribed on a throne in Adulis, Eritrea, describes an Aksumite king's conquests in the Red Sea region during the 3rd century.
The Geʽez script began as a vowel-less abjad. It developed into a vocalized abugida in the 4th century.

The 1st-century Roman Periplus of the Erythraean Sea asserts that the local ruler of Adulis could speak and write in Greek. Aksumite coins reflected the same Hellenism, with legends usually written in Greek, much like ancient Greek coinage.
The Hawulti Obelisk in Matara, Eritrea, dates tentatively to circa 400 CE, in the early Aksumite period. It bears an example of the ancient Geʽez script.

science.text: The Dartmouth study found that the mummified baboons were all born outside Egypt and were hamadryas baboons. This species is native to the Horn of Africa and the southwestern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which fits the long-debated location of Punt.
Coins showing the royal portrait began to be minted under King Endybis toward the end of the 3rd century CE, by which time Aksum had grown into a major power on the Red Sea.

A bronze sceptre or wand discovered at Atsbi Dera carries an inscription mentioning "GDR of Axum". Dated inscriptions from southern Arabia, which celebrate victories over a ruler called GDRT, were used to place that king around the beginning of the 3rd century CE.

In 2016, archaeologists excavated a basilica at Beta Samati in northeastern Ethiopia and radio-carbon dated it to the 4th century AD. It is the earliest known physical evidence of a church in sub-Saharan Africa, matching the time when King Ezana adopted Christianity.

In 2009, Andrew Kitchen, Christopher Ehret, Shiferaw Assefa and Connie Mulligan used Bayesian computational phylogenetics to model how Ethio-Semitic languages evolved. They concluded that Semitic arrived in the Horn between 1800 BCE and the Common Era, with a mean of 850 BCE.
science.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: Mani, founder of Manichaeism, listed Aksum in the 3rd century as one of the four great powers of his era. He named it alongside Persia, Rome and China. Its capital was the city of Axum.
The Kingdom of Aksum was considered one of the four great powers of the 3rd century by Mani, the founder of Manichaeism. He ranked it alongside Persia, Rome, and China.
Aksum adopted Christianity as its state religion in the mid 4th century under Ezana. Following their Christianization, the Aksumites ceased construction of steles.
The kingdom of dʿmt was a polity centred on Yeha in the Tigray Region, founded some time around 800 BCE. It is considered the first state in the region and the precursor to the Kingdom of Aksum.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: After dʿmt fell in the 5th century BCE, the plateau came to be dominated by smaller successor kingdoms. One of them rose during the 1st century and became the Aksumite Kingdom, which was able to reunite the area.

Under Gedara, who reigned c. 200 to 230, Aksum became the first kingdom of its line to be involved in South Arabian affairs. His reign brought control of much of western Yemen, including Najran and Zafar, until a joint Himyarite-Sabean alliance pushed the Aksumites out.
Ezana conquered Meroë in 330 for a short period of time. The Aksumites inherited from Meroë the Greek exonym "Ethiopia."

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes the ancient Somali city-states as decentralised, lacking a strong central government, with each port city administered by a tyrannical chief. Avalites was described as unruly, while the natives of Malao were more peaceful.
During the reign of Endybis, from 270 to 310, Aksum began minting coins. These coins have been excavated as far away as Caesarea and southern India.
Around the 5th century CE, Kush was weakened by internal rebellion amid worsening climatic conditions. It then disintegrated amid invasions by Aksum and the Noba into Makuria, Alodia, and Nobatia.
By the 2nd century, forces from Himyar invaded Avalites and put the town under siege. It would not recover until the advent of Islam centuries later.

philosophy.text: The Kingdom of Aksum was one of the first nations to officially accept Christianity. St. Frumentius of Tyre, called Abba Selama ("Father of Peace") in Ethiopia, converted King Ezana during the 4th century AD.

For much of the 1st millennium BC and 1st millennium AD, the predominant religion of proto-Somalis and other Cushites in the Horn was Waaq religion. Sources differ on whether Waaqism was henotheistic or monotheistic.

Around 316 AD, the brothers Frumentius and Edesius of Tyre sailed to Ethiopia with their uncle. Natives at a Red Sea port killed all the travellers except the two brothers, who were taken to court as slaves. They were given positions of trust and converted members of the royal court, and Frumentius became the first bishop of Aksum.
Many believe the Gospel reached Ethiopia even before Ezana's time. They point to the royal official said to have been baptised by Philip the Evangelist in chapter eight of the Acts of the Apostles.

The Physiologus, dated to around the 5th century AD, was one of the Greek texts translated and adapted into Ethiopian sapiential literature. This literature favoured narrative, parable, apothegm and rich imagery over abstract argument.
A coin dated to 324 shows that Ethiopia was the second country to officially adopt Christianity, after Armenia did so in 301. The religion may at first have been confined to court circles.

culture.text: The Kingdom of Aksum was one of the first countries in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion. This happened in the 4th century under King Ezana, after a man from Tyre named Frumentius converted him. In Ethiopia Frumentius is known as Abba Selama, meaning "Father of Peace".

For much of the 1st millennium BC and 1st millennium AD, a predominant religion among proto-Somalis and other Cushites in the Horn was Waaq religion. Later, in the post-classical period, various Abrahamic faiths became increasingly prevalent.

Before the fourth century, Ethiopia had a mixture of religions. Some people followed a religion that worshiped the serpent-king Arwe, while others followed what scholars call a Judaized form of religion. Christianity later took strong hold when Ezana declared it the state religion.

After Aksum became Christian, its people stopped building steles. The kingdom had entered the Greco-Roman cultural sphere through its position on the trade route between Rome and India. That connection helped lead Aksum to adopt Christianity in the mid 4th century under Ezana.

After Frumentius returned to Ethiopia by 331 AD, the rulers, who were not yet Christian, welcomed him. Ten years later, with the kings' support, most of the kingdom had converted. Christianity was then declared the official state religion.

Translating Scripture into Ethiopic (Ge'ez) let common people learn about Christianity. Many joined Syriac Christian missions and monasteries, where monastic rule stressed communalism, hard work, discipline, obedience and asceticism. Young people were especially drawn to the religion's mystical aspects.

In the Horn, ancient Waaqism may have been shaped by Abrahamic ideas. Scholars suggest tenets such as monotheism, non-tangible divinity, an ultimate destiny and omniscience may have influenced it. This contrasts with earlier worship at Laas Geel, which included the worship of cattle.

Ethiopian kings encouraged newly trained ministers to open schools in their parishes and educate their congregations. This gave the clergy more prestige and drew more people in. The Church grew from a royal cult into a widespread religion with a strong position in the country.

Some practices from the Waaq or classical era survive into the present, including mingis, a pre-Islamic demon-cleansing ritual. Those who practise mingis in Somalia face security risks: in July 2020, five people were killed in the country allegedly because they practised it. Elements of qabiilism, linked to ancestor veneration, and dabshid, which once included several practices associated with fire, are also suspected remnants of ancient Waaqism.
